content.text: The saved webpage path can store a URL, title, description, and metadata, and Memotron already has a vector resource and a local embedding worker. I also found a schema note describing this exact “horizontal infinite canvas with clusters” as a future graph view. That gives us a place to build from, though the current graph and embedding text need different inputs for the accuracy you described.

For Memotron, I’d treat this as a **semantic map of saved items**, with the current link graph as a separate view. Your example sets the right test: Orca, Synara, and Mono should be each other’s nearest neighbors because they center on managing coding agents; VS Code and Cursor belong in the broader coding-tools neighborhood. That distinction is supported by the products’ own descriptions. [Orca](https://www.onorca.dev/), [Synara](https://www.trysynara.com/), [Mono](https://www.usemono.dev/)

The accuracy will come mostly from **what Memotron knows about each bookmark and how it scores a pair**, not from the drawing algorithm:

1. **Build a concise profile for each saved page.** Use its title, description, relevant page content, and user notes to identify its primary purpose, workflows, and narrower category. A URL or title alone is too thin to reliably distinguish an agent workspace from a coding editor.
2. **Score closeness in two stages.** Use embeddings to find likely neighbors, then compare the strongest candidates using those purpose and workflow attributes. Give “both manage parallel coding agents” more weight than “both mention code.” Keep explicit user links as visible relationships, without making every linked item a semantic twin. Embedding retrieval followed by a more precise pairwise comparison is an established pattern. [Sentence Transformers documentation](https://www.sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/usage/usage.html)
3. **Learn from ordering examples.** Record judgments such as `similarity(Orca, Synara) > similarity(Orca, VS Code)` and include difficult near misses. Evaluate on held-out examples: nearest-neighbor accuracy, whether those orderings hold, and how often people correct a grouping. A general embedding benchmark alone cannot establish accuracy for Memotron’s meaning of “close.” [MTEB paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316), [hard-negative guidance](https://www.sbert.net/docs/package_reference/util/hard_negatives.html)
4. **Lay out the resulting neighbor graph on a pannable canvas.** Place close pairs together, give broader neighborhoods room between them, and retain existing coordinates when new bookmarks arrive so the map does not constantly reshuffle. Use clustering for labels and navigation, then render only the visible region.

There is one geometric limit: **a strictly one-dimensional horizontal line cannot faithfully represent all these relationships**. I recommend a two-dimensional map that feels horizontally infinite to navigate. Its coordinates communicate approximate neighborhoods; the underlying similarity score remains the source of truth for “how close.” UMAP is a candidate for initial placement, while G6 can render and refine the graph. [UMAP documentation](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html), [G6 force-layout documentation](https://g6.antv.antgroup.com/en/manual/layout/force-layout)

This fits the repository’s stated direction: [the graph enum](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/schema/product.type.ts:17) already describes a future horizontal canvas with clusters. The [current global graph](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/features/memory/graph/GlobalGraph.svelte:71) uses explicit links, so its force layout has no semantic closeness to work from. Memotron also has an embedding worker, but [vector generation](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/products/memotron/taco/taco.store.ts:12) is currently disabled and limited to markdown and headings; it does not yet cover the webpage bookmarks in your example. I’d first prototype the bookmark profiles and score against your five-item example and a larger reviewed set, then build the canvas around the scoring that passes those checks.

content.text: The distinction is clearer now: Memotron has collection-specific property values and link tags, but no general item-tag system; its “AI autofill” property is listed as disabled. I’d keep inferred attributes separate from user-confirmed properties, then let both help discover and explain nearby items.

You’re right on both points. I understood the canvas incorrectly, and a **strict embedding shortlist would be a recall bottleneck**: once it misses a pair, the later, more accurate comparison never sees it.

For the canvas, I’d use a 2D layout with **unbounded horizontal space and a fixed vertical range**. Users scroll left and right; clusters use both x and y within the visible height. The left-to-right order need not mean “more similar” or “older”—closeness is measured between items. We should keep positions stable as entries arrive, and expand horizontally when a neighborhood gets crowded.

For finding neighbors, I’d change the proposal to **multiple candidate paths whose results are combined**:

- Embedding similarity, calculated from a useful description of each item.
- Exact and keyword matches, including product terms and acronyms such as “ADE.”
- Shared capabilities and properties, such as *parallel agents*, *worktrees*, and *diff review*.
- Existing user links, collections, and confirmed tags.

Then score the **union** of those candidates in more detail. Hybrid keyword and vector retrieval is useful precisely because either method can surface items the other misses. [Elastic’s hybrid-search documentation](https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/hybrid-search)

For a modest personal library, we can compare each new item against *every* existing item with inexpensive signals; there is little reason to approximate that step. At larger scale, use indexes and periodically recheck poorly connected items. Even then, no retrieval scheme can guarantee discovery of a relationship that the captured content and user input give no evidence for. The product should let users link or move items, and use those corrections to improve future rankings.

**Auto properties and tags should be part of ingestion.** When a page is saved, extract a structured profile from its title, description, useful page content, and any user note:

| Kind | Example for Orca |
|---|---|
| Broad category | Developer tool |
| Narrow category | Agent development workspace |
| Capabilities | Parallel coding agents, worktrees, terminals, review |
| Suggested tags | Coding agents, multi-agent workflow |
| Evidence | The page text supporting each suggestion |

Use that profile for candidate discovery, scoring, cluster names, and an explanation such as “near Synara: both organize parallel coding agents and worktrees.” Normalize aliases so “ADE” and “agent development environment” do not become competing tags. Allow multiple categories and an **unknown** result when evidence is weak.

I’d distinguish *suggested* attributes from user-confirmed ones. Suggestions should carry a source and confidence, be editable, and never overwrite a user correction. In the current code, [collection properties](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/features/collections/collection.type.ts:185) are tied to collections, [link tags](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/schema/features.ts:188) describe links, and [AI autofill](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/features/collections/properties/property.store.ts:80) is disabled. So this needs a deliberate item-level design rather than treating existing link tags as bookmark tags.

The first accuracy gate I’d set is a reviewed set of saved items where **Orca–Synara–Mono rank closer to one another than to VS Code or Cursor**, plus cases where the right answer is *no confident cluster*. Measure both neighbor recall and tag precision before tuning the layout; a convincing picture cannot repair incorrect relationships.

Also consider that entries can not just be web pages but also user's markdown pages, voice recordings, web bookmarks, kindle highlights etc... the proximity algorithm should be intelligent enough to associate underlying concepts as well (We will use LLM with reasoning of course in the algorithm)
for example: if user came across an observation in a kindle book and came across similar observation in a web article - the in built AI serendipity engine built on top the graph should be able to find interesting correlations etc

I’ll connect those pieces into one design: pairwise judgments, reusable item profiles, precise comparisons, and discoveries across books, notes, audio, and web pages. I’ll check how Memotron stores those formats so the proposal accounts for what it can retain at capture time.

The current data model supports markdown text, Kindle highlight text, and optional audio transcription. Web bookmark capture mainly retains a title, description, and metadata. For the agent to compare items precisely without fetching them again, ingestion must retain enough source content and exact references to the passages behind each extracted claim.

The pairwise comparison becomes **more useful** in this design. It is the step that decides *what kind of relationship* two items have after several discovery methods have brought them together.

For example, a reviewer—either the user or an LLM examining source passages—might record:

- **Orca ↔ Synara:** close substitutes; both organize parallel coding agents.
- **Orca ↔ VS Code:** related developer tools, but different primary workflows.
- **Kindle highlight ↔ article passage:** the same underlying observation, perhaps expressed with different examples.

The ordering judgment `Orca–Synara closer than Orca–VS Code` helps calibrate future scores. User judgments are strong feedback; LLM judgments are predictions that retain their evidence and confidence. We would keep a *sparse* set of meaningful pair judgments, not compare every pair with an LLM or force all items into one global ranking. An LLM’s proposed relationship should point to the passages that justify it.

### One ingestion pipeline for every format

Each saved item needs a reusable, source-grounded representation:

1. **Preserve the source and its addressable parts:** markdown blocks, web sections, Kindle highlight and book location, or transcript segments with timestamps.
2. **Extract a structured profile:** topics, entities, activities, methods, tags, properties, and short claims or observations. Each extracted statement retains its source location, extraction version, and confidence.
3. **Index at several levels:** the whole item, its sections, and individual observations. Generate embeddings at the relevant levels, alongside keyword and structured indexes.
4. **Discover candidate relationships through multiple paths:** embeddings, shared concepts, exact terms, existing links, user properties, and periodic exploration. Have an LLM examine promising *source passages* to classify relationships such as **same idea, analogy, supports, contradicts, complements,** or **similar tool**.

That last distinction matters. A book and an article need not be close *as whole documents* because one highlight resembles one paragraph. Their **observations** can be strongly connected, and the graph can show that bridge between the parent items. Research on analogical reasoning also suggests that surface similarity alone can miss structural connections, while LLM reasoning still needs careful evaluation. [Analogical reasoning study](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.160/)

### Comparisons without repeated web research

The in-app agent should compare **saved evidence**, not restart research each time. If asked “Precisely compare Orca, Synara, and Mono,” it retrieves their cached profiles and the supporting source passages, then produces a table with consistent dimensions—primary purpose, agent orchestration, worktrees, editor, review workflow, and so on. Each substantive cell links back to the saved evidence. A missing value means **not established by the saved material**, rather than “the product lacks this feature.”

This requires a capture change. [Web capture currently retains mainly the title, description, and metadata](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/extensions/clipper/clipper.utils.ts:119), so those bookmarks alone cannot support a precise later comparison. Capture useful page text or a structured, cited snapshot **once**, with refresh when the user wants current information. Markdown text, [Kindle highlight text](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/features/memory/node/node.type.ts:897), and [audio transcription](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/features/memory/node/node.type.ts:362) provide other source paths. The [current chat](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/client/products/memotron/taco/Chat.svelte:21) searches one node, so it would need to retrieve evidence across items to serve this role.

### Serendipity is a second relationship mode

The proximity map should prioritize strong, understandable local neighborhoods. The serendipity engine should also look for **well-supported connections across neighborhoods**: the same principle in different fields, a useful counterexample, or two observations that complete each other. It can surface a card such as:

> “Your Kindle highlight and this article both suggest that constraints can improve creative decisions—but the book discusses individual choices while the article discusses team processes.”

Both quoted passages would be one click away. The engine ranks these suggestions by **evidence strength, novelty, and likely usefulness**; it does not make distant items appear adjacent merely because an LLM found an interesting analogy. This separation lets the map remain trustworthy while still enabling discovery. Graph-based retrieval systems similarly use extracted claims and relationships to answer questions beyond simple nearest-neighbor search. [Microsoft GraphRAG documentation](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/)

So the core design is a **source-backed concept and relationship index**. The horizontal map, comparison tables, and serendipity suggestions are three views over that same index.

*** Add File: /tmp/m-graph-backlog/issue.md
+## Executive summary
+
+Design and deliver the reusable Memotron "m graph" foundation: a source-grounded, multimodal concept and relationship index over saved items. It should make semantic proximity, precise cross-item comparison, and interesting cross-domain connections possible. The horizontal map, AI chat experience, and serendipity presentation are separate consuming-surface tickets.
+
+## Problem or opportunity
+
+Memotron saves webpages, markdown, audio, Kindle highlights, and other nodes, but the current global graph visualizes explicit links rather than inferred conceptual relationships. Web bookmarks currently retain mainly title, description, and metadata; that is insufficient for later precise comparison without re-fetching. A single item embedding or strict embedding-only shortlist can miss narrower product distinctions and analogous observations across different media.
+
+## Expected outcome
+
+A versioned, permission-aware index of source evidence, item profiles, concepts/claims, and explainable typed relationships. A new item can be enriched once, related to existing content through multiple discovery methods and selective LLM reasoning, and served to separate map, AI comparison/chat, and serendipity consumers without routine live web research.
+
+## Goals
+
+- Define ingestion adapters and stable source anchors for webpage snapshots, markdown blocks, transcript segments with timestamps, Kindle highlights with book/location context, and other supported node types.
+- Derive editable suggested tags and properties, normalized concepts, and short source-backed claims while keeping model inferences distinct from user-confirmed values.
+- Index whole items and granular evidence units; combine semantic, lexical, structured-facet, and explicit-link candidate discovery. Never make embeddings or inferred tags the sole eligibility gate.
+- Classify selected pairs by relationship type and evidence: same idea, analogy, support, contradiction, complement, substitute, or broader-topic relatedness. Record sparse user ordering judgments and model assessments separately.
+- Expose versioned graph/query contracts for neighborhoods, evidence-backed comparison, concept bridges, and feedback. Preserve deletion, access, and sync boundaries.
+- Define measurable quality and operating criteria for candidate recall, relationship precision, tag quality, evidence coverage, correction handling, scale, and cost.
+
+## Non-goals
+
+- Building the horizontally scrollable 2D map, AI chat/comparison UI, or serendipity UX in this issue; each needs its own ticket and consumes this foundation.
+- Using or migrating the legacy DataFn vector table as the target design. Treat it as unrelated legacy state.
+- Claiming exact metric distances in a 2D display or using a web crawl at every question.
+- Automatically treating LLM-generated labels or relationships as confirmed user facts.
+
+## Acceptance criteria for the eventual foundation work
+
+- Each supported item type yields traceable source units and can be reprocessed idempotently after edits, transcription changes, or model upgrades.
+- The agent can retrieve a saved item's supporting evidence and answer a comparison with a value and source anchor for each supported claim, or explicitly report insufficient saved evidence.
+- Multi-path discovery finds reviewed close pairs even when one method misses them; a held-out evaluation includes Orca/Synara/Mono versus VS Code/Cursor and cross-format Kindle/web/voice/markdown examples.
+- The graph distinguishes item proximity from claim-level bridges and stores relationship type, evidence, confidence, provenance, and review status.
+- User corrections override generated suggestions without being clobbered by reprocessing; access changes and deletion remove or hide derived records appropriately.
+- Architecture, privacy, storage, sync, backfill, model versioning, evaluation baselines, and rollback are documented before implementation tickets are decomposed.
+
+## Dependencies and risks
+
+- Capture must retain sufficient page content or a cited snapshot once; current bookmark metadata alone cannot justify precise comparisons.

+# Ideation & Product Rationale: m graph
+
+Backlog issue: [{{ISSUE_ID}}]({{ISSUE_URL}})
+
+## Opportunity
+
+Memotron holds a user's memory across webpages, markdown, voice recordings, Kindle highlights, and other saved content. Explicit links and collections capture some relationships, but they do not reveal every close tool, repeated observation, useful analogy, or contradiction. The desired product is an evidence-based memory graph that helps a user find what is near an item, compare several items precisely, and encounter meaningful connections between apparently distant sources.
+
+This document captures the idea and product requirements. It does not authorize implementation of the map, AI chat, or serendipity interfaces.
+
+## Target users and jobs
+
+- A person saving many developer tools wants similar tools grouped at the right level of specificity, not merely by a broad word such as "coding."
+- A reader wants a book highlight connected to a comparable observation in an article, note, or recording, even when the sources use different vocabulary.
+- A researcher wants the in-app AI agent to tabulate how saved items differ using retained evidence, without routinely starting a fresh web search or Firecrawl-like extraction.
+- A user wants automatically suggested tags and properties that are useful immediately, can be corrected, and do not silently replace their own organization.
+
+## Example journeys
+
+### Discover a close tool neighborhood
+
+The user saves onorca.dev, trysynara.com, usemono.dev, VS Code, and Cursor. The first three should normally form a tighter local neighborhood because their primary workflows center on coding-agent environments or orchestration. VS Code and Cursor remain nearby as broader coding tools. The graph must avoid declaring all five equally close just because they mention software development. A detail panel can explain the strongest shared and differing capabilities using saved evidence.
+
+This is a reviewed ordering example, not a universal hard-coded rule. Actual page content and product positioning can change, and the user may organize items for a different purpose.
+
+### Compare saved items precisely
+
+The user asks, "How do Orca, Synara, and Mono differ?" The AI agent returns a table of comparable dimensions, with source links for each substantive value. It distinguishes "not established by what I saved" from "does not have this capability." It may offer an explicit refresh when saved webpage evidence is missing or stale; repeated live research is not the normal comparison path.
+
+### Find an observation across formats
+
+The user highlights an observation in a Kindle book and later saves a web article or voice recording expressing a related principle. The graph identifies the specific highlight and article paragraph or transcript segment, not merely that a whole book and article share a topic. The user sees whether the passages state the same idea, support one another, disagree, or form an analogy, and can inspect both originals.
+
+### Correct and refine
+
+The user changes a suggested tag, rejects a weak relationship, or records that one pair is closer than another for a given anchor item. The correction remains user-owned through reprocessing and improves ranking or future evaluation. A generated suggestion is visibly distinct from a confirmed choice.
+
+## Product principles agreed in the discussion
+
+- **Evidence before placement.** The item and claim graph is the source of truth; a canvas is a navigation view over it.
+- **Several meanings of relatedness.** Close substitutes, shared themes, same observations, analogies, complements, and contradictions must not collapse into one unexplained score.
+- **No strict embedding gate.** Embeddings help discover candidates but may miss acronyms, niche product distinctions, negation, or cross-domain analogies. Candidate sets also come from lexical terms, structured concepts/properties, existing links, and broader exploration.
+- **Granularity matters.** A single matching highlight need not make an entire book visually adjacent to an article. Passage- or claim-level links can bridge larger items.
+- **Retain enough at capture time.** Fast later comparisons need saved source text and stable source references. Metadata-only bookmarks do not support precise evidence claims.
+- **User authority.** Automatic tags, properties, and pair judgments are suggestions. User corrections and explicit relationships keep distinct provenance and take precedence for user-facing organization.
+- **Serendipity has a different objective from proximity.** Strong local similarity organizes the map. Interesting, supported connections can bridge distant neighborhoods without moving them together.
+- **The old DataFn vector table is legacy.** It is not a target schema or architectural constraint for m graph.
+
+## Consuming surfaces, for separate tickets
+
+### Horizontally scrollable map
+
+A two-dimensional canvas uses an unbounded horizontal coordinate and a bounded vertical range, so the user navigates mainly left and right. Local neighborhoods have compact, readable placement; clusters gain horizontal room as they grow. The visual layout should remain stable when new items arrive. Distance is approximate and need not make the horizontal axis itself semantically meaningful. The surface consumes neighborhoods, cluster labels, explanations, and typed links from m graph. Building the interaction, virtualization, zoom, navigation, and visual design belongs in a separate ticket.
+
+### AI chat and comparison
+
+The agent asks m graph for saved profiles, evidence units, comparisons, and provenance. It can build tables on consistent dimensions and cite source anchors. It should state when a field is absent from saved evidence and distinguish a cached snapshot from a current live fact. Conversational UI, prompt interaction, table rendering, and optional explicit refresh belong in a separate ticket.
+
+### Serendipity engine and presentation
+
+The engine looks for well-supported links across neighborhoods: similar principles in different media, useful analogies, contradictions, and complementary ideas. It ranks suggestions by evidence quality, novelty, and likely user usefulness, then lets the user inspect and correct them. Notification timing, cards, discovery feeds, and recommendation controls belong in separate tickets.
+
+## Ideas and tradeoffs
+
+- **Proposal: normalize content into source units and short claims.** This supports accurate comparisons and cross-format association but adds extraction cost and versioning work.
+- **Proposal: item profiles plus claim-level relationships.** Item profiles make navigation efficient; claims prevent broad topic overlap from masquerading as a precise insight.
+- **Proposal: sparse pairwise LLM review and user ordering judgments.** Selected comparisons improve precision and calibrate ranking. Comparing every item pair with an LLM is not viable at scale.
+- **Proposal: automatic multi-label concepts and tags.** Broad and narrow labels can coexist, with aliases normalized. Weak evidence should permit "unknown" rather than forcing a category.
+- **Rejected: embedding-only top-k as a hard filter.** It can permanently exclude true relationships before deeper reasoning sees them.
+- **Rejected: one undifferentiated "related" edge.** It cannot explain a substitute versus an analogy or contradiction.
+- **Rejected: routine question-time web recrawling.** It introduces latency, cost, changing answers, and a dependency on third-party page availability.
+
+## Desired outcomes and success signals
+
+Quality thresholds are an **Open question**; do not infer a launch target from this document. Evaluation should include:
+
+- Recall of human-reviewed relationships in the union candidate set, including cases missed by embeddings alone.
+- Pair ordering accuracy on held-out triplets such as Orca/Synara versus Orca/VS Code, with hard near misses.
+- Precision and correction rate for relationship type, automatically suggested tags, and properties.
+- Source-coverage rate for claims and table cells; unsupported assertions and false "does not have" statements should be counted separately.
+- Cross-format discovery of observation-level matches, analogies, and contradictions across markdown, Kindle, voice, and web content.
+- Stability of neighborhoods as new items arrive, plus usefulness and dismissal rates for serendipity suggestions.
+- Latency, storage, inference cost, reprocessing time, and offline availability for realistic personal libraries.
+
+## Constraints and non-goals
+
+- Protect private saved content and honor resource access scope before indexing or retrieval.
+- Do not make a fabricated answer appear certain when source text is missing, truncated, or stale.
+- Do not turn model-inferred properties into user-confirmed collection values without an explicit product rule.
+- This issue defines the shared graph foundation. The map, chat, and serendipity features are described only as consumers and will receive separate execution tickets.
+- No requirement here to reuse the legacy DataFn vector resource or its current worker behavior.
+

+
+1. Which source types and capture paths are required for the first release, and how much webpage content may be retained?
+2. Should the system run extraction locally, in the account service, or in a user-selectable hybrid mode for private content?
+3. What is the durable boundary between inferred global item facets and collection-specific property values?
+4. Which relationship types and confidence levels are understandable enough to expose to users?
+5. How should a user's rejected link, positive link, or ordering judgment alter a personal graph versus the shared model?
+6. What corpus size, cost ceiling, and quality target should govern initial rollout?
+
+## Product acceptance criteria for planning
+
+- The documented journeys can be supported from saved source evidence, including source anchors, without mandatory question-time web fetches.
+- The model distinguishes close item neighborhoods from claim-level bridges and exposes a reason for each significant connection.
+- User-confirmed and model-suggested tags/properties/relations are identifiable and correctable.
+- The separate consumer surfaces can be specified against stable graph/query contracts.
*** End Patch";

+
+Backlog issue: [{{ISSUE_ID}}]({{ISSUE_URL}})

+## Scope and status
+
+This is a **proposal** for the reusable Memotron concept and relationship foundation. It records current repository evidence and design decisions from the discussion; storage format, model provider, thresholds, and deployment mode remain open. The horizontally scrollable map, AI chat/comparison experience, and serendipity presentation consume this foundation but are separate implementation tickets. +
+- `client/features/memory/graph/GlobalGraph.svelte` derives edges from explicit node links. `GlobalGraphUsingG6.svelte` renders a G6 force layout. It does not model semantic proximity.
+- `schema/product.type.ts` already notes a future horizontal canvas with clusters. Memotron's graph is composed by `client/products/memotron/overview/`.

+- New memory capability behavior belongs to the named memory owner under `client/features/memory`; inference transport belongs to `client/runtime`, durable client data to `client/datafn`, shared schemas to `schema`, and account-side sync/service code to `services/account` when needed. Product feature gates and final wiring remain in the product/composition layer. Portable presentation stays in `@21n/ui` only when domain-free.
+
+## Proposed system shape
+
+```text
+source node + retained source snapshot
+  -> modality adapter -> addressable evidence units
+  -> LLM extraction -> profiles, facets, entities, claims, suggestions
+  -> lexical + semantic + structured + explicit-link indexes
+  -> union candidate discovery -> selective pairwise LLM judgment
+  -> typed evidence-backed relations + neighborhood/clustering service
+  -> map / AI comparison-chat / serendipity consumers
+```
+
+The model reasons during extraction and selected pair review. Embeddings provide broad candidate discovery and inexpensive similarity; they are not the only route to a candidate or the final authority on a connection. All derived records carry model/extractor version, source version, confidence, and review provenance.
+
+## Proposed records and invariants
+
+Names below are conceptual contracts, **not a decision to place them in a specific table**.
+
+| Record | Minimum contents | Invariant |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Source snapshot | Owner/resource ID, type, capture time, content hash, retained text or secure reference, access scope, extraction state | Never claim a page feature beyond available saved evidence; mark changed/stale snapshots. |
+| Evidence unit | Stable unit ID, source ID, exact text or permitted reference, heading/block/path, page/location or audio start/end, parent context | Every extracted claim and comparison citation resolves to a source unit. |
+| Item profile | Item ID, concise purpose, broad/narrow categories, capabilities, entities, summary, quality state | Multi-label and uncertain; missing information remains unknown. |
+| Claim or observation | Normalized proposition, qualifiers, stance/modality, source evidence IDs, context, confidence | Preserve negation, scope, and attribution; a model paraphrase is not itself source evidence. |
+| Suggestion | Proposed tag/property value, canonical label ID or alias, evidence IDs, confidence, state | User-confirmed values and rejected suggestions are distinct; reprocessing cannot overwrite them. |
+| Relationship | Source/target item or claim IDs, typed relation, directional flag if needed, scores, evidence pairs, model version, review state | A topic-level match cannot be presented as claim-level agreement. |
+| Judgment | Anchor/positive/negative or pair rating, judge type (user/model), context, rationale, evidence, timestamp | User feedback is not conflated with model-generated pseudo-labels. |
+| Layout projection | View/version, item IDs, coordinates, cluster membership and label | Derived view data; does not define semantic truth or index membership. |
+
+All persisted records need stable identities, permission scope, an idempotent source/version key, and deletion/update semantics. Decide whether some records are local only, synchronized, or recomputable caches before finalizing physical schema. A schema or physical database change will require the repository's DataFn mapping and forward-migration workflow.
+
+## Ingestion and source handling
+
+1. A capture or edit event identifies the node type, owner, content version, and whether the source is complete enough to process. Deduplicate equivalent URLs/resources without merging distinct user annotations.
+2. A modality adapter produces evidence units. Markdown uses block/heading IDs and spans; web uses retained cleaned page sections and URL/heading anchors; Kindle highlights use exact text plus book and page/location; audio uses transcript segments with timestamps and transcription quality metadata. Other media require an explicit adapter and an unsupported/partial state until they have reliable evidence.
+3. An LLM extracts profiles, candidate facets/tags, entities, and atomic observations from bounded units plus local context. Validate structured output, deduplicate aliases, and retain links to exact source spans. Keep broad and narrow categories; allow abstention when evidence is weak.
+4. Index item summaries and evidence/claim units separately. Include full text/lexical terms, normalized facets and entities, source relations, and newly chosen semantic representations. Retain the embedding model and content versions so an index can be rebuilt consistently.
+5. Schedule relation discovery after indexing. Prioritize newly changed units, neighborhood repair, and periodic exploration of isolated or low-confidence items.
+
+**Decision from discussion:** precise cached comparison requires useful page content saved once. A metadata-only bookmark can participate at lower confidence, but the system must say when there is insufficient evidence. A live fetch is an explicit refresh action or a separately defined ingestion step, not routine question-time work.
+

+
+Use the **union** of independent candidate sources: exact/lexical search, item and passage embeddings, normalized concept/facet overlap, existing explicit links, user-confirmed tags/properties, and controlled exploration. Do not exclude pairs solely because an embedding or generated tag is absent. For a modest personal library, inexpensive exact comparisons with every existing item can avoid approximate-index misses; the scale transition and threshold are open questions.
+
+Selectively ask an LLM to compare evidence for promising or uncertain pairs. Output structured relation type, shared/different dimensions, support IDs on both sides, confidence, and an "insufficient evidence" path. Review can record that A is closer to B than C for the anchor A. Such triplets tune and test the ranking; they do not imply a universal total ordering or directly fix canvas coordinates. User judgments carry greater authority than model assessments for that user's organization. Keep only sparse material pair judgments, not a quadratic all-pairs LLM corpus.
+
+Separate scores for **proximity** (similar purpose or same concept), **claim correspondence** (agreement, conflict, analogy), and **serendipity** (supported connection across otherwise distant topics, with novelty and usefulness). An item with one matching passage can have a bridge link without being forced into the other item's entire neighborhood. Explicit user links may influence discovery and context without automatically proving semantic closeness.
+
+## Clustering and graph projection
+
+Build neighborhoods from high-confidence item relationships and broader topic hierarchy; keep claim/observation bridges as typed cross-neighborhood edges. Allow multiple memberships where useful and leave weakly evidenced items unclustered. Explain cluster labels using representative evidence, not generated tags alone. The map consumer may initialize a 2D layout from semantic neighborhoods and stabilize it incrementally; the x direction is navigational, while y remains bounded to the viewport. Do not promise that absolute pixel distance preserves every high-dimensional relation. Coordinates, viewport virtualization, interaction, and exact render technology belong to the separate map ticket.
+

+
+Proposed capability APIs, with exact signatures **not yet defined**:
+
+- `getNeighborhood(itemId, scope, version)`: nearby items, cluster membership, relation types/scores, explanations, evidence references, and unknown/partial states.
+- `compareItems(itemIds, dimensions?, scope, snapshotPolicy)`: aligned, evidence-backed dimensions and citations; return unknown where saved content cannot justify a value. The chat surface can then synthesize a table without routine web retrieval.
+- `findConceptLinks(itemOrClaimId, relationTypes?, diversityPolicy)`: observation-level connections, including analogies and contradictions, with exact source anchors.
+- `recordFeedback(judgment, scope)`: user confirmation, rejection, tag correction, or anchor-specific ordering; never mutate source evidence implicitly.
+- `getIndexStatus(itemId)`: not indexed, partial, ready, stale, or failed, with a safe retry/reindex path.

+
+- **Open question:** local-only, cloud-backed, or selectable processing/storage. The source's access scope must govern snapshots, derived claims, vectors, relations, and prompts in every mode.

+- Version extractors, taxonomies, embedding models, scoring policies, and layout projections. Support bounded background reindexing, partial-result states, restart recovery, and rollback to a previous read model if a new model degrades quality.

+

+
+1. **Evidence contract and evaluation corpus:** sample all target modalities and document stable anchors, missing-content states, access rules, and reviewed close/false/analogy/contradiction examples.
+2. **Capture and enrichment foundation:** retain suitable source content, normalize evidence units, derive profiles/claims/suggestions, and establish versioned persistence and reprocessing.
+3. **Discovery and relation quality:** multi-path candidate union, sparse LLM pair review, human feedback, relation types, and evaluation against the corpus.
+4. **Read APIs and operational hardening:** graph/query contracts, permissions, update/delete propagation, bounded jobs, observability, migration/rollback, and performance limits.
+5. **Separate consumer tickets:** horizontal map, AI comparison/chat, and serendipity presentation independently consume verified APIs.

+
+- Build a held-out human-reviewed set spanning close substitutes, broader-category neighbors, hard negatives, cross-format same-idea matches, analogies, contradictions, and genuinely unrelated items.

**Recommendation:** build m graph as a reusable, provider-backed derived-index capability using Superfunctions contracts, while keeping the authoritative saved items and user choices in DataFn. The product owns its modality adapters and policy; a possible future Superfunction package could own extraction/projection interfaces, candidate fusion, typed relations, versioned jobs, and graph queries. The current `@memoryfn/core` candidate is scoped agent memory and embedding retrieval, not a ready-made personal content graph; evaluate it for pieces, not as the graph system of record.

Nucleum derives those fields in `schema/search.provider.ts` and connects SearchFn to local IndexedDB and server OpenSearch. DataFn's `SearchProvider` and plugin interfaces support search and mutation hooks. The concrete SearchFn DataFn provider is lexical: it maps record text to SearchFn documents and does not implement neural embedding or typed graph reasoning. The `semantic` query type in the broader interface does not make this provider a semantic index.
- **Declarative scopes:** introduce a versioned, schema-checked m graph projection manifest keyed by DataFn resource, such as `node -> { lexical: [label,text,notes], evidence: [body,mdText,...], semanticProfiles: [item,claim], access: ownerScoped }`. Existing `indices.search` remains the lexical declaration. Keep embedding model, dimensions, provider credentials, and refresh policy in provider configuration, since they are deployment choices. A first-class `indices.semantic` DataFn annotation can be proposed upstream after the contract proves reusable; it must be a new meaning, not the legacy `indices.vector` resource.
- **Maintenance contract:** an authoritative create/update/delete or permission change produces a durable, ordered-by-resource projection event after commit. A worker reads the current revision, checks access policy, builds evidence units and embeddings, and writes versioned projections idempotently. Track checkpoint, retry/dead-letter state, tombstones, and rebuild generation. A stale job must not overwrite a newer revision. Deletion and access revocation must hide results immediately at query time, even while projection cleanup runs. Content-hash and model-version keys avoid repeated embedding work. Index/model upgrades use shadow generations and atomic read-side switch after catch-up.
- **Why a new lifecycle contract is needed:** current DataFn `afterMutation` hooks are fail-open and may run around local/remote reconciliation; they are appropriate to enqueue a hint, but are not a durable exactly-once projection feed. Sync imports, backfills, restores, and cross-device changes also require explicit coverage. An outbox or resumable change log is a proposed Superfunctions/DataFn extension. Do not perform LLM calls on the synchronous user-write path.
- **Provider boundaries:** SearchFn contributes lexical candidates; a semantic adapter contributes item/claim nearest neighbors; structured facets and explicit links contribute additional candidates; m graph fuses candidates and asks an LLM to judge selected pairs against cited evidence. DataFn stores authoritative user records and user-confirmed decisions. m graph stores rebuildable evidence/profile/edge projections with provenance and model versions. Its query API returns ranked neighbors, typed relations, confidence, and source anchors, not just IDs. Every query intersects current DataFn permissions and deletion state.

A hybrid mode is possible, but the manifest must make provider egress and E2EE limitations explicit. Never send decrypted E2EE material to a hosted embedder without an explicit product policy and user action.

This is an architecture proposal, not a claim that the current Superfunctions packages already provide the complete pipeline. **Recommendation:** start with an on-demand, versioned cache for eligible public web pages, not an attempt to crawl or store the whole internet. This can avoid duplicate fetch, parsing, extraction, and embedding when many users save the same public page. Keep the service distinct from each user's saved bookmark, annotations, links, ranking feedback, private capture, and graph projection.

```text
user-owned DataFn bookmark (private membership, capturedAt, annotations, chosen version)
    -> optional public source reference (canonical URL + content version)
shared public corpus (eligible fetch, sanitized snapshot, extracted units, reusable embeddings)
    -> account-scoped m graph projection (personal claims, edges, judgments, permissions)
```

- **Three independent reuse keys:** normalize URLs conservatively (redirects and canonical hints are evidence, not proof of identical content); identify immutable page versions by content hash plus locale/variant; identify extraction and embedding artifacts by content hash plus parser/prompt/model version. A changed page creates a new version. Preserve the user's captured version for precise citations and comparisons; a refreshed public version must not silently rewrite what the user saved.
- **Admission rule:** only content obtained through an unauthenticated public fetch and passing the service's access, robots, response-cache, and retention policy may enter the shared corpus. A page captured from an authenticated tab, paywall, personalized response, intranet/private IP, tokenized URL, or user-added annotation is private regardless of apparent URL overlap. URL hashes are not privacy protection because popular URLs are guessable. Never use cross-user cache hits or counts as a user-visible signal.
- **Operations:** conditional revalidation with ETag/Last-Modified when supplied; time-to-live and freshness policy by source; rate limits and SSRF protection; content-size limits; parser-version rebuilds; content removal/takedown; immutable provenance (`requestedUrl`, final URL, fetchedAt, content hash, parser version, source offsets). Apply publisher/copyright/retention policy separately from robots and HTTP cache directives. RFC 9111 defines shared-cache restrictions such as `private`/`no-store`; RFC 9309 defines robots behavior. Neither alone grants broad rights to republish content.
- **Private fallback:** if a page is ineligible for sharing, retain a user-scoped snapshot/derived record under the agreed privacy policy. If only public metadata was captured, comparisons must say that evidence is insufficient instead of fabricating page details. Where E2EE or local-only processing is selected, client-side content should not be uploaded to the shared corpus.
- **Service boundary:** a distinct public-content service/abstraction can own fetching, canonicalization, immutable snapshots, reusable extraction, and cache invalidation; DataFn remains authoritative for user membership and permissions. The graph may reference a public version but should not rely on the global store as its only evidence copy until retention and availability guarantees are established.
- **Adoption gate:** measure duplicate eligible URLs/content hashes, mean processing cost per public page, cache hit rate, refresh rate, storage/egress cost, and privacy exclusions. Begin with per-page on-demand cache; expand only when measured reuse exceeds operating and compliance cost. Public corpus access must never bypass account-scoped query authorization.

External references: [Google canonicalization guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization), [RFC 9111 HTTP caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html), [RFC 9309 robots exclusion](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html).

Yes to both, with distinct boundaries. I added these recommendations to the [m graph architecture](https://linear.app/21n/document/architecture-and-delivery-plan-tidy-481-m-graph-cf4572c086aa) and [ideation](https://linear.app/21n/document/ideation-and-product-rationale-tidy-481-m-graph-6985cf9be71a) docs and verified the updates.

### 1. Build m graph with Superfunctions abstractions

DataFn already declares full-text fields through `indices.search`, and Nucleum connects those declarations to SearchFn indexing ([schema](</Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/schema/search.provider.ts:71>)). That is a good pattern for m graph. The [current SearchFn provider](</Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions-dev/searchfn/datafn-provider/src/index.ts:87>) indexes and retrieves text; it does not generate neural embeddings or judge conceptual relationships.

I recommend a **versioned m graph projection declaration** per resource: which fields supply searchable text, which supply citable evidence, how to split each modality into units, and which units may be embedded or sent to an external model. DataFn remains the authority for saved items and user decisions. SearchFn supplies lexical candidates; an embedding provider supplies semantic candidates; m graph combines them and stores evidence-backed, typed relationship judgments. This design does not depend on the legacy vector table.

Index maintenance needs more than today’s plugin hook. DataFn’s [`afterMutation` hooks](</Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/superfunctions-dev/datafn/core/src/hooks.ts:56>) are fail-open, so a failed graph job could be lost. The proposed Superfunctions extension should use a durable change log or outbox, idempotent workers, revision checks, deletion handling, and rebuildable index versions. LLM work then runs outside the save operation.

### 2. Share processing for eligible public websites

A separate **on-demand public page cache** is likely worthwhile when users save the same pages. It could reuse a public fetch, extracted text, and embeddings. Each user’s bookmark, captured page version, annotations, links, and graph judgments stay private.

The cache should distinguish a URL from a *particular version of its content*: canonical URLs can group duplicates, but they do not prove two captures are identical ([Google’s canonicalization guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization)). A comparison must still cite the version the user saved. Authenticated or personalized pages must stay outside the shared corpus; shared HTTP caching also has explicit restrictions for responses marked `private` or `no-store` ([RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html)). Public fetching needs a separate crawling and retention policy ([RFC 9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html)).

I’d begin with an on-demand cache and measure repeated eligible pages, processing savings, freshness cost, and privacy exclusions before building a broader web database. No repository code was changed.

content.text:
## 1. Extracting and storing an entry’s profile

I’d use **three storage layers**:

| Layer | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| **DataFn, authoritative** | The saved entry and source snapshot; user-confirmed tags, property values, links, and corrections. These must survive any reindex. |
| **m graph profile store, derived** | The extracted profile, suggested tags and properties, concepts, claims, evidence references, confidence, and extraction version. Persist it for fast use, but make it rebuildable from the source. |
| **Search and embedding indexes, derived** | Lexical entries and vectors keyed to profile or evidence-unit IDs, with content and model versions. |

So the profile should be **persisted separately from the main entry**, but it should be a structured graph record, not merely a blob inside a vector index. When a user accepts a suggested tag or corrects a property, that decision becomes authoritative DataFn data. Re-extraction must respect it.

For each new entry, the pipeline would create citable units first: page sections, markdown blocks, transcript timestamps, or Kindle locations. An LLM then extracts a structured profile with purpose, narrow and broad categories, capabilities, differentiators, entities, and any supported observations. Every factual value points back to evidence; unsupported fields remain unknown. For example, the narrow category **agent development environment** could distinguish your first three bookmarks from the broader **coding IDE** category of VS Code and Cursor. Separate embeddings for the item’s purpose and its individual observations preserve both close neighborhoods and surprising cross-format connections. Candidate retrieval and selective pairwise judgments then refine relationships beyond what the profile alone can express.

Re-run extraction when the source changes, using source revision and extractor version. Reuse unchanged units and embeddings. Keep the old profile identifiable as stale until the new projection is ready.

## 2. Comparison with Memgraph, Mem0, and GraphRAG

| System | Where it fits | Difference for m graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Memgraph** | A graph database that can combine vector search and graph traversal in one engine. [Memgraph documentation](https://memgraph.com/vector-search) | It could store and query our derived relationships. Choosing it would not define how Memotron extracts profiles, handles private source versions, judges proximity, or preserves user corrections. I would choose a graph database when measured traversal and scale needs justify it. |
| **Mem0** | A memory system that extracts entities, links memories through them, and blends those links with vector and keyword ranking. Its current platform graph is built in rather than requiring an external graph store. [Mem0 Graph Memory](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/blob/main/docs/platform/features/graph-memory.mdx) | It is the closest analogy for automatic memory connection. Mem0 says its current graph connections are based on shared entities and do not carry typed entity relationships. |
| **Microsoft GraphRAG** | An indexing and question-answering pipeline that extracts text units, entities, relationships, and claims, then builds communities and summaries. [Indexing overview](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/index/overview/), [query modes](https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/query/overview/) | It offers the strongest reference pattern for evidence units and corpus-level reasoning. Our system additionally needs continuous per-entry updates, personal proximity judgments, user feedback, and a stable interactive map. Its community summaries could help chat, but they do not determine where two saved items belong on that map. |

My recommendation is to **borrow GraphRAG’s evidence-centered extraction pattern, Mem0’s incremental memory-connection ideas, and evaluate Memgraph only as a possible storage engine**. **Yes—PostgreSQL is enough to start** for DataFn records, the shared public-page cache, m graph profiles and relationships, and embeddings via pgvector. PostgreSQL also has full-text search, so m graph does not need a separate graph or vector database at the outset. pgvector supports exact nearest-neighbor queries; add an approximate index only when measured query time warrants its recall trade-off, especially for user-scoped searches. [pgvector documentation](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/blob/master/README.md), [PostgreSQL text-search indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-indexes.html).

“One database” can still mean **separate tables with separate responsibilities**. I would keep derived profiles, evidence units, embeddings, and edges out of the main node row, keyed by source ID and revision. Keep large original files, such as audio, in their authoritative file store; PostgreSQL can hold their references and extracted text. This does not use the legacy DataFn vector table.

**Your rederivation model is right, with one qualification:** the authoritative inputs are:

1. DataFn records: saved entries, access rules, user-confirmed tags and properties, explicit links, and user judgments.
2. The **exact retained source content**: a pinned, immutable version in the public-page cache for eligible web pages; a private snapshot or file for personalized pages, recordings, and other private material.
3. Versioned extraction rules and model configuration.

A URL pointing to today’s page is insufficient to rebuild what the user saved last month. If a public-cache version may be deleted, retain a user-owned source snapshot or accept that exact rederivation is unavailable. The m graph profile, embeddings, and machine-generated edges can then be rebuilt from those inputs; user corrections cannot be treated as disposable projections. For end-to-end encrypted content that the server cannot read, derivation must run where it can be decrypted.

I’d build this as a **local, read-only pilot against your Memotron data**, with its own PostgreSQL projection. It can later read from DataFn without making the undeployed DataFn system a prerequisite.

The AWS inventory for your account gives us a useful starting size: **33,815 node records, about 4,663 likely top-level memory entries, 2,551 web pages, 69 audio nodes, 246 images, and 30 PDFs** in `ap-south-1`. The account also has a large mutation and activity history; those records should not become map items. Most saved web pages have metadata or descriptions, but not full article text. I made no AWS writes or local code changes during this inventory.

| Stage | Build and verify |
|---|---|
| **1. Reproducible backfill** | Export the account’s Memotron nodes, links, collections, properties, and file references into a versioned local snapshot. Reconstruct parent/child content so a markdown page becomes one map entry with its blocks as evidence. Fetch referenced media from S3 where available. Record IDs, hashes, failures, and source timestamps. |
| **2. Evidence extraction** | Give web pages, markdown, clips, audio, images, and PDFs separate extractors that produce a common evidence format: passages or observations with source locations. Fetch public pages through an interchangeable extractor; use the Aside Browser for exceptional pages, then replace that adapter with Firecrawl or similar in production. Keep the captured page version so later comparisons do not require another crawl. |
| **3. Profiles and graph** | Generate structured per-entry profiles: concepts, user-meaningful tags, typed properties, claims, entities, intended use, and evidence references. Store them as **derived PostgreSQL tables**, alongside embeddings, relation edges, pairwise judgments, model versions, and job status. Keep the Dynamo snapshot and captured public-page content as rederivation inputs. |
| **4. Accuracy loop** | Retrieve candidates from the **union** of embedding neighbors, lexical matches, shared entities/properties, existing links, and exploratory candidates. Have a reasoning model compare selected pairs on explicit dimensions, save the judgment and cited evidence, then calibrate against a hand-reviewed set. An embedding miss must not permanently exclude a pair. |
| **5. Local consumers** | Build a read-only local MCP server for search, neighborhoods, connection explanations, evidence, and cited comparison tables. Build the horizontally scrolling map from the same graph projection, with bounded vertical placement and stable cluster positions as new entries arrive. |

For models, I’d benchmark a small set of DigitalOcean **open-weight** reasoning models and a vision model against the same labeled examples before choosing one. DigitalOcean’s current catalog lists serverless open-weight reasoning and vision choices. I did not find a speech transcription model in its catalog; Cloudflare already offers [Whisper Large V3 Turbo](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/whisper-large-v3-turbo/), so I’d test that before operating a Whisper droplet. Cloudflare’s [Qwen3 embedding model](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/qwen3-embedding-0.6b/) is a candidate for the embedding stage, subject to retrieval testing. [DigitalOcean model catalog](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/models/)

**First milestone:** backfill and profile roughly 150 varied top-level entries, including your ADE/IDE example, sparse bookmarks, long markdown pages, and cross-format matches. Measure candidate recall, pairwise judgment quality, evidence accuracy, comparison completeness, and inference cost. Then run the full Memotron corpus with checkpointed jobs. The map should be evaluated on whether nearby items are useful neighbors; a 2D layout cannot preserve every semantic distance exactly.

I would make the local MCP answer comparison questions from stored claims and source passages, with citations and a clear “insufficient evidence” result when a page was not successfully enriched. That is the key to precise tables without repeated browsing. The existing Memotron map is geographic, while the old infinite-grid code is an experiment, so this prototype should be a separate consumer of the graph projection rather than a modification of the current product UI.

Two practical details for implementation: the legacy file path goes through S3 ([server/s3v2.ts](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/nucleus/server/s3v2.ts)), and the current shell has no DigitalOcean or Cloudflare inference credentials configured. Also, this account’s node inventory contained no Kindle highlights, so that cross-format case needs a separate evaluation fixture even though the extractor should support it.

-Local development lives here. +Local development lives here. The pilot reads one user's legacy Memotron data from DynamoDB, stores derived graph records in hosted PostgreSQL, and stores source snapshots and extraction artifacts in a private Cloudflare R2 bucket. The horizontal map and local MCP server can consume the same projection.
+
+## Pipeline
+
+The source stage reads only the six Memotron partitions (`node`, `file`, `link`, `collection`, `property`, `linkTag`) for the configured user. Each DynamoDB query page becomes a compressed, hashed R2 object and is upserted into the dedicated PostgreSQL schema. Page checkpoints make reruns resumable. The source partitions are not a transactional point-in-time snapshot; use a fresh run to catch later edits.
+
+The projection stage identifies top-level entries, treats the legacy `$NONE` reference sentinel as empty, and folds child blocks into cited evidence. Public-page HTML, owned file media, profiles, embeddings, and pair judgments are separately versioned derivations. An entry's source hash and each derivation's source hash determine whether it needs recomputation. Raw fetched page and media bytes go to R2; PostgreSQL holds searchable text, structured profiles, a 1,024-dimensional pgvector projection, and relation judgments. The legacy vector DataFn schema is unused.
+
+Candidate relations are the union of vector neighbors, lexical matches, explicit links, and shared extracted concepts. DO reasoning judges candidates and persists a 0-1 proximity score, relation type, explanation, and supporting entry IDs. The evidence profile captures concepts, tags, properties, claims, and uncertainty for later chat and comparison surfaces. Thin title-only records remain marked `thin` and should not be treated as fully understood.
+
+## Run
+
+Use Python 3.10 or newer when available. The local code is small; no source snapshots or media are written to local disk.
+
+```sh
+python3 -m pip install -e .
+python3 -m mgraph migrate
+python3 -m mgraph backfill
+python3 -m mgraph project
+python3 -m mgraph enrich-web --limit 20
+python3 -m mgraph enrich-audio --limit 1
+python3 -m mgraph enrich-image --limit 1
+python3 -m mgraph enrich-pdf --limit 1
+python3 -m mgraph profile --limit 10 --model glm-5.3
+python3 -m mgraph embed --limit 10
+python3 -m mgraph relate --limit 5 --model kimi-k3
+python3 -m mgraph status
+```
+
+`--entry node:<id>` selects specific entries for enrichment, profiling, and embedding. `relate --left node:<id> --right node:<id>` judges a specific pair. Public page extraction can be partitioned with `--shard 0 --shards 4` through shard 3. Successful derivations are skipped on rerun. An omitted `--limit` processes every eligible item and may entail substantial external API usage.
+
+`python3 -m mgraph evaluate` runs four fixed synthetic relation cases against GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 and writes `evaluation.json`. This checks JSON validity, evidence IDs, proximity ordering, latency, and token cost. It is a smoke test, not a labeled corpus evaluation. A user-reviewed test set from actual Memotron entries is still needed before treating the scores as accuracy measurements.
+
+The media extractor reads only S3 URLs in the configured user's legacy `tidyfiles` bucket. It prefers an optional OpenAI-compatible Whisper endpoint on a DigitalOcean GPU Droplet when `MGRAPH_DO_TRANSCRIPTION_URL` is set; otherwise it uses Cloudflare Workers AI Whisper Large V3 Turbo. The DO serverless model catalog currently has no dedicated transcription endpoint. The `phidata` profile currently receives S3 403 for the legacy file bucket, so audio, image, and PDF extraction require a credential with object read access or an authenticated legacy download route. Existing transcripts and source metadata are still indexed.
*** End Patch"));

# m graph pilot evaluation

Measured September 27, 2026. The four fixed cases in `evaluation.json` test output shape, evidence IDs, coarse relation labels, and proximity ordering. They are synthetic and too small to estimate production accuracy. The real-account comparison used saved Orca and Synara pages after public-page extraction and GLM-5.3 profiling.

| Model | Fixed labels | Ordering | Fixed-call time | Estimated fixed-call cost | Real Orca/Synara relation |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| GLM-5.3 | 3/4 | pass | 22.44 s | $0.004182 | `same_niche`, 0.85 |
| Kimi K3 | 4/4 | pass | 41.86 s | $0.028485 | `same_niche`, 0.88 on the same profile format |

GLM called the synthetic ADE pair `same_product` instead of `same_niche`, though it ranked that pair closer than a general coding IDE. Kimi distinguished the labels. On the real saved pages both labels were correct. The real pair's GLM call took 9.24 seconds and about $0.004482; the corresponding Kimi call took 23.9 seconds and about $0.021333. The latest persisted Kimi relation after the final root projection remains `same_niche` at 0.87. Output token counts and latency vary between requests; these figures are observations, not guarantees.

The pilot should use GLM-5.3 for routine profiling and relation judgments, then send uncertain or high-impact pairs to Kimi K3 as a second opinion. A larger user-reviewed set with hard negatives, cross-medium conceptual echoes, and page-content hallucination checks is required before tuning proximity thresholds. DigitalOcean's [serverless pricing](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/pricing/) lists GLM-5.3 at $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output tokens, versus Kimi K3 at $3.00 and $15.00. Cached input is billed at lower rates and is recorded separately by the pipeline.

## Transcription economics

The source contains 69 audio nodes with 94.67 recorded minutes. Forty-five lack a transcript, totaling 72.47 minutes. At Cloudflare's [Whisper Large V3 Turbo rate](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/whisper-large-v3-turbo/) of $0.000513 per audio minute, transcribing every missing recording is approximately **$0.03718**; retranscribing all audio would be approximately **$0.04856**. Billing can differ if duration metadata is inaccurate or clips are split and retried. The Cloudflare endpoint passed a synthetic WAV probe; enabling voice activity filtering made a silent probe return empty text instead of a spurious transcript.

DigitalOcean's [serverless model catalog](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/models/) does not list a dedicated ASR model. Nemotron 3 Diarization supplies speaker labels but no words. An optional OpenAI-compatible Whisper endpoint can be hosted on a DO GPU Droplet and selected through `MGRAPH_DO_TRANSCRIPTION_URL`. DO's [GPU Droplet pricing](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/pricing/) starts at $0.76/hour for RTX 4000 and $1.57/hour for L40s; credits may cover that bill, but provisioning and maintaining a GPU endpoint for this account's roughly four cents of missing Cloudflare transcription is more work than the pilot needs. The legacy file bucket currently denies the configured AWS identity, so no real recording has been transcribed yet.

Candidate density can change as the graph fills, so 34,000 is a sizing scenario rather than a fixed work count. A 10,000-20,000-pair budget gives a roughly $285-$465 successful-call baseline, with additional allowance needed for retries and unusually long entries.

A single sequential worker has been far below the minute ceilings, while a full graph can consume more than the then-reported daily remainder. content.text:
**Kimi K3 planning estimate:** the pilot has 4,901 entries still eligible for profiling. Applying the token usage measured from 80 completed profiles to Kimi K3’s [current rates](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/pricing/) gives **about $105 for profiles**. The 54 measured Kimi pair judgments average **$0.018 each**: about $180 for 10,000 pairs or $360 for 20,000. That puts a capped pass at **roughly $285–$465** before retries. If candidate-pair density stays near the current sample, judging every candidate would bring the baseline to **about $712**; I would plan for **$700–$1,000** in that scenario because long entries and retries vary. These figures cover profiles and pair judgments. Kimi vision reprocessing, embeddings, and hosting would add cost.

**Cloudflare transcription is configured and has run.** It produced 24 nonempty extractions; 21 recordings returned no detected speech and remain flagged. Processing the 72.47 minutes that lacked transcripts is about **$0.04 at list price**, rather than a confirmed billing total. [Cloudflare’s published rate](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/whisper-large-v3-turbo/) is $0.000513 per minute.

For the remaining run, Tier 4’s [published ceiling](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/limits/) is 360 requests/minute and 12 million tokens/minute. Live headers for the tested models showed **360 requests/minute, 3 million tokens/minute, and about 18 million daily tokens remaining at the probe**. I added bounded 429/503 retries, a 100,000-token daily reserve, and resumable checkpoints in [cli.py](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/cli.py:237). The practical approach is bounded batches with one worker first, then increase concurrency from observed headers. DigitalOcean says [capacity can still throttle within quota](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/limits/), so zero rate-limit responses cannot be guaranteed.

The four-case synthetic smoke test found these [DO-hosted alternatives](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/models/):

| Model | Exact labels | Takeaway |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Kimi K2.6 | 4/4 | Promising cheaper Kimi option; one label changed on repeat. |
| DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 | 3/4 | Fast, inexpensive candidate for real-pair evaluation. |
| MiMo V2.5 Pro | 3/4 | Valid output with more tokens; one label changed on repeat. |
| GLM-5.3 Flash | 3/4 | Very cheap candidate generator. |
| Nemotron 3 Ultra | 3/4 | Fast, with one conceptual-label miss. |
| Qwen 3.5 397B | Incomplete | Needed more output tokens; the longer run stalled. |

The measurements and limitations are in [EVALUATION.md](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/EVALUATION.md:18). I’d compare Kimi K3, K2.6, DeepSeek, and MiMo on reviewed **real Memotron pairs** before changing the judge. The new quota tests pass: **14/14**. Also check the account’s prepaid balance before a large run; [DO requires one for serverless inference](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/details/pricing/), and credit eligibility depends on the award.

content.text:
I reviewed **12 reproducibly random Kimi profiles** from the 317 completed when I sampled, plus two audio profiles because audio was rare in the random draw. I compared them with the stored source text and extractions.

**The main topics were captured well.** Product pages retained specific capabilities, a sparse Tableau bookmark stayed appropriately vague, and a personal idea was described as a proposal rather than a decided plan.

The sample also exposed problems that matter for the precise comparisons you want:

- **Citation accuracy:** Of 72 claims in the random sample, **4 Goodreads claims cite a child node with no supporting text**. The facts appear in the fetched parent page, but those claim links would lead an agent to the wrong evidence. Another **57 claims cite only the entry as a whole**, without a passage location.
- **Conflicting merged output:** A knowledge graph article profile says its definition is absent, although that definition is present in an earlier segment. Segment-specific uncertainty was retained after merging.
- **Structured data quality:** Some changing figures and prices are stored as properties without an “as of” date. Comparable fields also use different keys, such as `name` and `product_name`. An audio profile puts uncertain, phonetically transcribed place names into properties.
- **Presentation:** 11 of 12 summaries retain an unnecessary “Segment 1:” prefix.

**Assessment:** The profiles look promising for finding related concepts, but I would not yet rely on them for high-accuracy, citation-backed difference tables. I’d fix passage-level provenance and segment reconciliation, then normalize and date comparison properties before the large pair-judgment stage. This review checks profiles against stored extractions; it does not independently verify the original pages, images, or audio. The profiling run is still active.

content.text:
The dominant causes are **evidence formatting, validation, and merge logic**. A better prompt would help, but increasing reasoning effort alone would leave the clearest defects intact.

| Gap | Cause in the current pipeline | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong claim citation | The model receives allowed IDs, including child nodes with no text. The validator checks that an ID is allowed, not that it supports the claim. | Give each source passage a stable ID; require a supporting excerpt; verify the excerpt belongs to that passage. |
| Contradictory uncertainty | The [merge code](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/cli.py:305) unions segment uncertainties without reconciling them against the whole entry. It also inserts “Segment 1:”. | Reconcile after merging and remove that prefix. |
| Inconsistent properties | The prompt requests a freeform object, with no shared field names, source, or observation date. | Store normalized property records with evidence, confidence, and an “as of” date where relevant. |
| Uncertain audio names | Profiling receives a transcript but no field-level transcription confidence. | Keep uncertain names out of definitive properties until checked against the audio. |

I would tighten the prompt **after** changing that structure: distinguish observed facts, vendor claims, and inferences; require a quote for each claim; and omit unsupported or time-sensitive property values. Then test the revised pipeline on the failure cases and a broader held-out sample before rederiving profiles.

The current [Kimi request](/Users/serro/Documents/dev/n/agent/experiments/mgraph/mgraph/cli.py:240) does not set reasoning effort. DigitalOcean documents `reasoning_effort` for supported models, and a small live Kimi K3 request with `max` succeeded, but that does not establish an accuracy gain. [DigitalOcean reasoning documentation](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/inference/how-to/use-reasoning/), [Kimi effort levels](https://www.kimi.com/code/docs/en/kimi-code/models.html)

My recommendation is to **fix and measure the pipeline first**, then compare default and `max` effort on ambiguous profiles and pair judgments. The existing `profile-v3` output would need rederivation after a profile change; the 20,000-pair stage should use the validated version.

content.text:
I manually inspected **11 randomly selected current profiles** across web pages, Markdown, image, audio, PDF, and video, then screened **25 more random web profiles** for identity mismatches.

The profiles generally captured useful concepts and handled uncertainty well. All 11 passed the pipeline’s structural quote check. But I found a **material quality gap**: an Edgedive bookmark was enriched with Struct page content, and the resulting profile identifies the entry as Struct. A saved ChatGPT conversation was likewise profiled from a generic public ChatGPT page, losing the saved conversation’s subject. Another bookmark appears to have encountered a changed product page.

The quote check cannot catch this: a quote can match the *fetched* text exactly while that text belongs to the wrong page or an unauthenticated fallback. In the current 628 v7 profiles, **50 have multiple `name` values**, **105 have no `name`**, and **81 record that unsupported quoted facts were removed**. Missing names are sometimes reasonable for sparse notes; multiple names need review before precise comparisons.

**Assessment:** concept extraction looks promising, but I would add a saved-entry versus fetched-page identity check and detect login or generic fallback pages **before embeddings and pair judgments**. The current audit does not catch those errors. I made no changes to the running job.
proceed

I’ll pause the profile workers at their resumable boundary, add checks for fetched pages that conflict with the saved entry or show a login fallback, then resume profiling and verify the audit catches those cases. I’ll also make the primary name a single value while retaining aliases as separate evidence.
